description: Test plans, test data types, and how to evaluate a finished spreadsheet against client requirements and HCI principles.
content_html:
Why Test?

A spreadsheet that looks correct is not the same as a spreadsheet that is correct. A formula might return the right answer for typical data but break when a user enters a zero, a very large number, or the wrong data type entirely. Testing is the systematic process of proving that the solution works as intended — and finding the problems that prove it does not. Skipping testing does not remove the bugs; it just means the client discovers them instead of you.

Testing happens in two phases: testing during development and testing after development. Both phases include technical testing (does the spreadsheet calculate correctly and behave as designed?) and usability testing (can the user navigate it without confusion?).

Key Fact

Three types of test data are used in a test plan: valid (typical, expected data that should be accepted), extreme (boundary values that are valid but at the edge of the acceptable range — should be accepted), and invalid / erroneous (data that should be rejected because it is outside the range or the wrong type). Extreme and invalid are not the same thing.

Understanding the Three Types of Test Data

Consider a sports-club fixtures spreadsheet where the goals scored field must accept whole numbers between 0 and 20. Valid test data would be a typical match score such as 3 — expected, inside the range, should be accepted without any error message. Extreme test data would be 0 and 20 — the boundary values. These are still valid (both are within 0 to 20) but they sit right at the edge where rounding-off mistakes in validation formulas often hide. Extreme values should be accepted; if they are rejected, the validation rule is wrong. Invalid / erroneous test data would be −1, 21, “five”, or a blank — all of these should be rejected and trigger an error message.

A well-prepared test plan uses all three types. Testing only with valid data tells you the spreadsheet works for normal use; it tells you nothing about what happens when a user makes a mistake. Testing only with invalid data tells you the error handling works; it tells you nothing about normal operation.

A test plan is a structured document with one row per test. Each row has seven columns:

Test number — a unique identifier so tests can be cross-referenced.
Test description — what is being tested (e.g. “Validate that the goals field rejects a value of −1”).
Test data — the exact data entered and its type (valid / extreme / erroneous).
Expected result — what should happen (e.g. “Error message displayed; cell value not updated”).
Actual result — what actually happened (filled in after running the test).
Remedial action — what was changed to fix a failure.
Retesting — confirmation that the fix was re-tested and the test now passes.

A test plan that has been followed correctly shows evidence of all seven columns filled in for every test. An empty “Actual result” column or a missing “Remedial action” entry tells the assessor that the test was planned but not completed.

What to Test

Technical testing covers three areas. First, navigation features: does every button, hyperlink and macro take the user to the correct worksheet? Does the start-up screen appear when the workbook opens? Can the user return to the main menu from every worksheet? Second, spreadsheet calculations: does every formula return the correct result for valid, extreme and erroneous inputs? Does the spreadsheet handle errors (such as a #DIV/0! caused by a blank cell) gracefully? Third, content in outputs: does the printed or displayed output show the correct data, in the correct format, following the house style from the design?

Usability testing checks that the interface is clear and logical to a typical user — not just to the developer who built it. A user who has never seen the spreadsheet before should be able to open it, enter data, navigate to the output, and print a report without needing to ask for help. If they cannot, the learnability of the design has not been achieved.

Key Fact

The seven columns in a test plan document are: test number, test description, test data, expected result, actual result, remedial action, and retesting. Evidence in all seven columns is required for a thorough, well-documented test plan.

When and How to Retest

When a test fails, you fix the problem and then retest that specific test to confirm the fix worked. You may also need to retest any other tests that could have been affected by the change — for example, fixing a formula in one worksheet might break a multi-sheet reference in another. Document the remedial action and the retest outcome in the test plan; do not simply delete the original failed result.

After testing, you evaluate. Evaluation is not just a list of what worked. A comprehensive evaluation explains how effectively the solution meets each requirement and why — using evidence from the testing phase.

Evaluate against two areas. First, client requirements: go back to the original brief. Does the solution calculate everything the client asked for? Are the outputs in the format the client needs? Has house style been followed consistently? Is the navigation system the client described in the brief actually present and working?

Second, HCI design principles: consider learnability (does a first-time user find it intuitive?), memorability (is the layout consistent enough for a returning user?), accessibility (is colour contrast sufficient, are names meaningful, are screen tips present?), and layout (is white space used well, are controls in logical positions?). Each HCI point should be evaluated against what was designed in the planning phase — did the finished solution match the wireframes?

A basic evaluation merely states “the total calculation works”. An adequate evaluation describes how effectively it works. A comprehensive evaluation explains why it is effective — for example: “The VLOOKUP formula correctly retrieves the hourly rate for all 15 tested employees, therefore the weekly pay totals are accurate, which means the client can use the output directly for payroll without manual checking.”

What Evaluation Does Not Include

The evaluation for this unit does not include user feedback, focus-group reviews, or user acceptance testing. Those are separate processes used in professional software development but they are not part of this assessment. Your evaluation is based on your own systematic comparison of the finished solution against the original design and the client requirements — not on survey responses or comments from other students.
exam_tip_html: The most common error in evaluation questions is giving a list of what works without explaining why it meets the client’s requirements. Always use a connective: “therefore”, “which means that”, or “because”. For test-data questions, never describe extreme data as invalid — extreme values are at the boundary but they are still valid and must be accepted. If a question asks you to choose test data for a specific range, always give the exact numbers and name the type (valid / extreme / erroneous) for full marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Three types of test data are used in a test plan: valid (typical, accepted), extreme (boundary, accepted), and invalid/erroneous (outside range or wrong type, rejected) — each plays a distinct role and they are not interchangeable.
  • A complete test plan document has seven columns: test number, test description, test data, expected result, actual result, remedial action, and retesting; all seven must be completed for every test.
  • Evaluation must cover both client requirements and HCI design principles, explaining effectiveness with reasons and evidence — not just stating what worked.

practice_questions.text: Which type of test data sits at the boundary of the acceptable range and should be accepted by the spreadsheet?
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for: B — Extreme.
A: Valid — this is typical, in-range data, not boundary data.
B: Extreme — CORRECT. Boundary values that are valid but at the edge.
C: Invalid — this should be rejected.
D: Erroneous — this is data of the wrong type and should be rejected.

practice_questions.text: State what should be recorded in the 'remedial action' column of a test plan.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: what was changed / fixed to correct a failed test / the action taken to resolve the failure.

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between testing during development and testing after development.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Testing during development catches errors as each section is built, before moving on, so problems are fixed incrementally; testing after development checks the completed solution as a whole against all requirements. Secure: During = while building; after = when complete. Developing: Names both without explaining the difference. Emerging: Describes one only.

practice_questions.text: Describe what a developer should do when a test in the test plan fails.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: identify and fix the error / apply remedial action. 1 mark for: retest the affected test (and any tests that may have been affected by the change) and record the outcome in the test plan.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a developer should test a validation rule that accepts ages from 16 to 65 with the values 15, 16, 65, 66, and 'thirty'.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies all three test data types with correct examples AND explains the reason for each, using connectives. E.g. 16 and 65 are extreme (boundary) values, therefore testing them confirms the validation rule handles the edges correctly, because this is where off-by-one errors most often occur. 15, 66 are invalid (outside range) and 'thirty' is erroneous (wrong data type), so testing them confirms the rule rejects data it should not accept. Secure: Identifies two types with reasoning. Developing: Identifies data types but limited reasoning. Emerging: States the values should be tested.

practice_questions.text: A student has completed a spreadsheet solution for a school canteen. Their evaluation states: 'The solution works well and meets the client's requirements.' Discuss how comprehensive this evaluation is, and describe what a better evaluation would include.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–9): Identifies why the existing evaluation is inadequate (no evidence, no HCI coverage, no connectives, no reference to specific requirements); outlines both areas (client requirements AND HCI design principles); provides developed examples of what stronger evaluation looks like; reaches a justified conclusion. E.g. The evaluation is at the basic level because it states that requirements are met without describing how or why. A comprehensive evaluation would compare each client requirement against the solution — for example, explaining that the COUNTIF formula correctly calculates the number of meals sold per day, therefore the client can use it for stock ordering. It would also evaluate HCI principles: whether learnability was achieved by checking whether a first-time user could navigate from start-up to the invoice output without help, and whether memorability was supported by consistent button placement across all worksheets. A strong evaluation uses test-plan evidence to support every judgement and uses connectives to make the reasoning explicit. Secure (5–6): Covers both areas with some development. Developing (3–4): Covers one area or gives superficial treatment of both. Emerging (1–2): Identifies the evaluation is weak without developing why.

knowledge_checks.q: A validation rule accepts values between 1 and 50. Which of the following is an example of extreme test data for this rule?
Which column in a test plan records what was changed after a test failed?
_____ test data is data that falls outside the acceptable range or is the wrong data type, and should be rejected by the spreadsheet.
Evaluation must cover two areas: client requirements and _____ design principles.
Match each test data type to the correct description.
right: Data of the wrong type (e.g. text in a numeric field), should be rejected
Typical, expected data within the acceptable range, should be accepted
Boundary value at the edge of the acceptable range, should be accepted

flashcard_questions.a: Boundary values at the edge of the valid range — should be accepted.
Data of the wrong type or format — should be rejected by the spreadsheet.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the seven columns in a test plan document.
flashcard_questions.a: Test number, description, test data, expected result, actual result, remedial action, retesting.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens after a test fails in the test plan?
flashcard_questions.a: Apply remedial action, then retest and record the new outcome.
Whether a typical user can navigate and operate the solution without specialist knowledge.
Navigation features, spreadsheet calculations, and content in outputs.

flashcard_questions.q: What two areas must a spreadsheet evaluation cover?
flashcard_questions.a: Client requirements and HCI design principles.

flashcard_questions.q: What makes an evaluation comprehensive rather than basic?
flashcard_questions.a: It explains effectiveness with reasons and evidence, not just states what worked.

flashcard_questions.q: Does evaluation for this unit include user feedback or focus groups?
flashcard_questions.a: No — evaluation is the developer's own comparison against requirements, not survey responses.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is testing during development important?
flashcard_questions.a: It catches errors early, before they affect other sections being built.

glossary_terms.definition: Testing carried out while the spreadsheet is still being built, to catch errors before moving on to the next section.
Testing carried out on the completed spreadsheet to confirm it meets all requirements before being handed over to the client.
A document recording every planned test, the data used, the expected result, the actual result, and any action taken to fix a failure.
Testing that checks whether a real user can navigate and operate the solution effectively, without specialist knowledge.
A structured judgement of how well the finished spreadsheet meets the client's requirements and HCI design principles.
